name: Pheromone sprays (Human Pheromone Sciences)

lead: Pheromone sprays are commercial fragrance products sold on the claim that they contain human sex pheromones that raise the wearer's attractiveness. Human Pheromone Sciences is named as a seller of such products.

Proponents say the compounds signal attraction. Researchers report that no pheromonal substance has been shown in peer-reviewed studies to directly influence human behavior, and describe the field as speculative and controversial. The studies in the entry's source search concern insect pheromones, not humans.

paras: Buyers apply the spray like a cologne or add it to their usual scent, usually before social outings or dates. Users judge results by the reactions they perceive.
No specific harms were found in the sources reviewed; as with any fragrance, skin irritation or allergy is possible. The main concern cited is that the attraction effect has not been demonstrated.

angle.text: Buyers spray these products hoping the claimed pheromones make them seem more attractive to others. Peer-reviewed research has not shown that human pheromones change behavior, so the effect rests on marketing and anecdote.

lead: Pheromone sprays are commercial fragrance products marketed as containing human sex pheromones that make the wearer more attractive to others. Human Pheromone Sciences is named as a seller of such products, and people use them in the way they use colognes and body sprays: applied before meeting people, in the hope that scent will increase attraction.[1]

The idea draws on research into chemical signals in animals and on small studies of compounds such as androstenol and androstadienone in humans. Wikipedia reports that no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behavior, and describes the field as one with small samples, publication bias and mixed results.[1]

Studies found under the term pheromone spray concern insects, such as microencapsulated sex pheromone sprays used on codling moths and queen pheromone sprays used on honey bee crops, rather than human products.[2][3]
infobox: No peer-reviewed human study has shown a pheromone directly influences behavior[1]

paras: Reported findings include androstenol and androstadienone studies on perception and attention, menstrual synchrony claims later questioned, and MHC-linked odor preferences.[1] A 1978 study had participants wear masks treated with androstenol and rate pictures; those exposed rated the pictures as warmer and friendlier.[1] Another study applied androstadienone to the upper lip of 50 men and women and reported an attention shift toward emotional facial expressions; women reacted more positively and men more negatively.[1]

Reviewers cite small samples, publication bias and poor methodology, and note the human vomeronasal organ receptor genes are nonfunctional pseudogenes; whether chemicals reach the brain through that organ or other tissue is disputed.[1]
Advertisers claim body sprays contain human sexual pheromones acting as an aphrodisiac; Wikipedia describes the claims as not supported by peer-reviewed evidence.[1]
No studies found of these commercial products. Pheromone spray research located concerns insects such as codling moths, honey bees and carpenter ants.[2][3][4]
